claim: Spontaneous slow oscillation-associated slow wave activity is characterized by alternations of network quiescence and stereotypical episodes of neuronal activity.
source: Spontaneous slow oscillation-associated slow wave activity represents an internally generated state which is characterized by alternations of network quiescence and stereotypical episodes of neuronal activity - slow wave events.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the characteristics of slow wave activity.

claim: Optic fiber-based calcium recordings of local neural populations in cortex and thalamus can detect neurophysiologically defined slow calcium waves in isoflurane anesthetized rats.
source: We used optic fiber-based calcium recordings of local neural populations in cortex and thalamus to detect neurophysiologically defined slow calcium waves in isoflurane anesthetized rats.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Individual slow wave events can be used for event-related analysis of simultaneously acquired whole-brain BOLD fMRI.
source: The individual slow wave events were used for an event-related analysis of simultaneously acquired whole-brain BOLD fMRI.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: BOLD responses are directly related to onsets of slow calcium waves.
source: We identified BOLD responses directly related to onsets of slow calcium waves, revealing a cortex-wide BOLD correlate: the entire cortex was engaged in this specific type of slow wave activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the event-related fMRI analysis.

claim: The entire cortex is engaged in slow wave activity.
source: We identified BOLD responses directly related to onsets of slow calcium waves, revealing a cortex-wide BOLD correlate: the entire cortex was engaged in this specific type of slow wave activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrating cortex-wide activation.

claim: Findings were confirmed for ongoing slow wave activity by independent component and seed-based analyses.
source: These findings demonstrate a direct relation of defined neurophysiological events to a specific BOLD activity pattern and were confirmed for ongoing slow wave activity by independent component and seed-based analyses.
evidence: This describes the validation of the primary findings using alternative analytical methods.

claim: Slow oscillation-associated slow wave activity arises from neuronal populations in deeper cortical layers.
source: Slow oscillation-associated slow wave activity is characterized by a waxing and waning of spontaneous neuronal firing arising from neuronal populations in deeper cortical layers (Chauvette et al., 2010; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Stroh et al., 2013), influencing neuronal excitability as well as stimulus-response properties of neuronal networks throughout the brain (McGinley et al., 2015b; Petersen et al., 2003; Steriade et al., 1993c; 1993b).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Slow wave activity influences neuronal excitability and stimulus-response properties of neuronal networks throughout the brain.
source: Slow oscillation-associated slow wave activity is characterized by a waxing and waning of spontaneous neuronal firing arising from neuronal populations in deeper cortical layers (Chauvette et al., 2010; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Stroh et al., 2013), influencing neuronal excitability as well as stimulus-response properties of neuronal networks throughout the brain (McGinley et al., 2015b; Petersen et al., 2003; Steriade et al., 1993c; 1993b).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The slow wave rhythm is a 'default mode' of cortical network activity.
source: The slow wave rhythm as a 'default mode' of cortical network activity (Sanchez-Vives and Mattia, 2014) stands in contrast to the rather desynchronized, persistent state during rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep and active wakefulness, dominated by low amplitude and high frequency cortical activity (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; McGinley et al., 2015a; Steriade et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sanchez-Vives and Mattia, 2014.

claim: Slow wave activity stands in contrast to the desynchronized, persistent state during REM sleep and active wakefulness.
source: The slow wave rhythm as a 'default mode' of cortical network activity (Sanchez-Vives and Mattia, 2014) stands in contrast to the rather desynchronized, persistent state during rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep and active wakefulness, dominated by low amplitude and high frequency cortical activity (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; McGinley et al., 2015a; Steriade et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations comparing different brain states.

claim: Persistently active neuronal population activity can be maintained by sedation.
source: A similar persistently active neuronal population activity can also be maintained by sedation (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Constantinople and Bruno, 2011.

claim: The low frequency (<1 Hz) component of field potential recordings during slow wave activity reflects bimodality with active phases and silent periods.
source: During slow wave activity, the corresponding low frequency (<1 Hz) component of field potential recordings reflects bimodality: active phases, in which cells are depolarized and silent periods with rather hyperpolarized membrane potentials (Timofeev et al., 2001), likely influenced through neuromodulatory pathways (Eggermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Timofeev et al., 2001 and Eggermann et al., 2014.

claim: Slow oscillation is highly similar across cortical regions.
source: This oscillation is highly similar across cortical regions (Ruiz-Mejias et al., 2011), and also across species, from lizards to humans (Achermann and Borbély, 1997; Buzsáki et al., 2013; Eschenko et al., 2006; Mölle et al., 2002; Shein-Idelson et al., 2016; Steriade et al., 2001), suggesting well-defined conserved roles (Destexhe et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations demonstrating similarity across regions and species.

claim: Slow oscillation is similar across species, from lizards to humans.
source: This oscillation is highly similar across cortical regions (Ruiz-Mejias et al., 2011), and also across species, from lizards to humans (Achermann and Borbély, 1997; Buzsáki et al., 2013; Eschenko et al., 2006; Mölle et al., 2002; Shein-Idelson et al., 2016; Steriade et al., 2001), suggesting well-defined conserved roles (Destexhe et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations demonstrating cross-species similarity.

claim: Slow waves propagate in anterior-posterior direction over the cortical surface, recruiting large cortical areas.
source: It has been shown that slow waves are propagating, most of the times in anterior-posterior direction over the cortical surface, eventually recruiting large cortical areas (Busche et al., 2015; Massimini et al., 2004; Stroh et al., 2013), resembling a travelling wave, likely mediated by recurrent excitatory activity (Luczak et al., 2007; Massimini et al., 2004; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing slow wave propagation.

claim: Slow wave propagation is likely mediated by recurrent excitatory activity.
source: It has been shown that slow waves are propagating, most of the times in anterior-posterior direction over the cortical surface, eventually recruiting large cortical areas (Busche et al., 2015; Massimini et al., 2004; Stroh et al., 2013), resembling a travelling wave, likely mediated by recurrent excitatory activity (Luczak et al., 2007; Massimini et al., 2004; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and uses the qualifier 'likely', indicating it is a supported hypothesis.

claim: Slow wave activity can be found in sub-cortical regions such as the thalamus and hippocampus.
source: In addition, slow wave activity – correlated to cortical slow wave events - can also be found in sub-cortical regions such as the thalamus (Stroh et al., 2013) and the hippocampus (Busche et al., 2015; Hahn et al., 2006), probably mediated by long-range excitatory connections (Leong et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing subcortical slow wave activity.

claim: Subcortical slow wave activity is probably mediated by long-range excitatory connections.
source: In addition, slow wave activity – correlated to cortical slow wave events - can also be found in sub-cortical regions such as the thalamus (Stroh et al., 2013) and the hippocampus (Busche et al., 2015; Hahn et al., 2006), probably mediated by long-range excitatory connections (Leong et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and uses the qualifier 'probably', indicating it is a supported hypothesis.

claim: Slow wave activity of a spatially confined neural population can be detected by optic fiber-based calcium recordings.
source: Slow wave activity of a spatially confined neural population can be detected by optic fiber-based calcium recordings (Adelsberger et al., 2014; Grienberger et al., 2012; Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing the methodology.

claim: OGB-1 stains both neurons and astrocytes.
source: Besides neurons, OGB-1 also stains astrocytes (Garaschuk, 2013), yet population-based recordings are dominated by neuronal action potential related calcium influx (Grienberger et al., 2012; Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Garaschuk, 2013.

claim: Population-based calcium recordings are dominated by neuronal action potential related calcium influx.
source: Besides neurons, OGB-1 also stains astrocytes (Garaschuk, 2013), yet population-based recordings are dominated by neuronal action potential related calcium influx (Grienberger et al., 2012; Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grienberger et al., 2012 and Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012.

claim: Calcium transients acquired by optic fiber result from synchronous spiking of at least 30 cells at the recording site.
source: Calcium transients acquired by the means of an optic fiber result from synchronous spiking of at least 30 cells at the recording site (Grienberger et al., 2012) and represent the integrated signals obtained mainly from neurons and the surrounding neuropil, as demonstrated by simultaneous two-photon calcium imaging (Grienberger et al., 2012; Schulz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing the cellular basis of the optical signal.

claim: Optic fiber-based calcium recordings represent integrated signals obtained mainly from neurons and the surrounding neuropil.
source: Calcium transients acquired by the means of an optic fiber result from synchronous spiking of at least 30 cells at the recording site (Grienberger et al., 2012) and represent the integrated signals obtained mainly from neurons and the surrounding neuropil, as demonstrated by simultaneous two-photon calcium imaging (Grienberger et al., 2012; Schulz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies using two-photon calcium imaging.

claim: BOLD fMRI provides a measure of brain-wide hemodynamic signals.
source: BOLD fMRI provides a measure of brain-wide hemodynamic signals.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BOLD fMRI.

claim: The BOLD signal reflects changes in blood oxygenation, regional cerebral blood flow, and regional cerebral blood volume.
source: The BOLD signal reflects changes in blood oxygenation, regional cerebral blood flow, and regional cerebral blood volume, linking these hemodynamic parameters to neuronal activity by neurovascular coupling.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the BOLD signal.

claim: Resting state fMRI is increasingly employed to study large-scale correlations of brain activity fluctuations in low frequency bands.
source: Resting state fMRI (Biswal et al., 1995; Fox and Raichle, 2007; Hutchison and Everling, 2014) is increasingly employed to study large-scale correlations of brain activity fluctuations in low frequency bands.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing resting state fMRI applications.

claim: Neuronal correlates of spontaneous fluctuations in the BOLD signal have been identified by combining fMRI and LFP recordings.
source: Neuronal correlates of spontaneous fluctuations in the BOLD signal have been identified by combining fMRI and LFP recordings at rest, subsequently correlating these two signals (Chang et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2016; Magri et al., 2012; Pan et al., 2013; Shmuel and Leopold, 2008; Thompson et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior combined fMRI-LFP studies.

claim: Previous studies did not detect fMRI signal responses directly related to individual slow wave events.
source: However, those studies used resting state fMRI methods to spatially map signal fluctuations which correlate to infra-slow fluctuations of the LFP signal, but they did not detect fMRI signal responses directly related to individual slow wave events.
evidence: This statement contrasts the current study with prior work, highlighting a gap in the literature.

claim: Hemodynamic fluctuations have been correlated with wide-field calcium imaging of excitatory neurons.
source: Others correlated hemodynamic fluctuations with wide-field calcium imaging of excitatory neurons, convolving these two signals (Ma et al., 2016b) or compared functional connectivity during different, temporally transient patterns of calcium activity (Matsui et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2016b and Matsui et al., 2016.

claim: Lower-frequency hemodynamic fluctuations were not well-predicted by calcium signals in previous studies.
source: While these results support the notion of resting-state hemodynamics being coupled to underlying patterns of excitatory neuronal activity, particularly lower-frequency hemodynamic fluctuations were not well-predicted (Ma et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2016b.

claim: Globally detected calcium signals are linked to hemodynamic functional connectivity.
source: Evidence was found that globally detected calcium signals are linked to hemodynamic functional connectivity and that the spatial information of the cortical network functional connectivity may be embedded in the phase of global calcium waves (Matsui et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Matsui et al., 2016.

claim: It has not been investigated which cortical network activity reflected by the hemodynamic BOLD signal underlies the active phase of the slow wave rhythm.
source: Nevertheless, it has not been investigated until now, which cortical network activity reflected by the hemodynamic BOLD signal underlies the active phase of the slow wave rhythm – the slow wave event.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Optic fiber-based calcium recordings can be performed unperturbed by the magnetic field of the MR scanner.
source: To achieve this aim, optic fiber-based calcium recordings are well-suited as they can be performed unperturbed by the magnetic field of the MR scanner (Schmid et al., 2016; Schulz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schmid et al., 2016 and Schulz et al., 2012.

claim: Event-related fMRI analysis can be used to identify BOLD changes in response to individual events.
source: The key concepts of event-related analyses are time-locking and signal averaging. Although originally intended to reveal transient changes in brain activation associated with the presentation of discrete sensory stimuli, event-related analysis can detect BOLD activity upon any type of previously defined events (Huettel et al., 2009; Josephs et al., 1997), in our case the active phases of the optically recorded slow calcium wave activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing event-related fMRI methodology.

claim: A change of excitability state of a small population of neurons can be indicative for global network states reflected by whole-brain BOLD activity patterns.
source: Here we show that a change of excitability state of a small population of neurons can be indicative for rather global network states being reflected by whole-brain BOLD activity patterns, demonstrating the particular relevance of considering readouts of local population activity for fMRI measurements.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental results.

claim: Calcium waves were reliably recorded during simultaneous fMRI recordings in 8 out of 10 experiments.
source: Calcium waves were reliably recorded during simultaneous fMRI recordings (8 out of 10 experiments in 7 out of 8 animals), occurring at frequencies ranging between 9 and 15 events/min (mean 10.9 ± 1.3 events/min), in line with previous in vivo recordings (Busche et al., 2015; Kerr et al., 2005; Stroh et al., 2013) (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This statement reports experimental results with specific success rates.

claim: Calcium waves occur at frequencies ranging between 9 and 15 events/min (mean 10.9 ± 1.3 events/min).
source: Calcium waves were reliably recorded during simultaneous fMRI recordings (8 out of 10 experiments in 7 out of 8 animals), occurring at frequencies ranging between 9 and 15 events/min (mean 10.9 ± 1.3 events/min), in line with previous in vivo recordings (Busche et al., 2015; Kerr et al., 2005; Stroh et al., 2013) (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This statement reports quantitative experimental results.

claim: For OGB-1, calcium waves exhibited rise times of 72 ± 14 ms, durations of 1356 ± 85 ms, and amplitudes of 2.6 ± 0.1 Δf/f.
source: For OGB-1, the typical and rather uniform calcium waves exhibited sharp rise times (72 ± 14 ms, and rather variable durations and amplitudes of 1356 ± 85 ms and 2.6 ± 0.1 Δf/f, respectively (n = 30 traces, five animals).
evidence: This statement reports quantitative experimental results for OGB-1.

claim: For GCaMP6f (hSyn), the rise times exhibited slower kinetics (163 ± 14 ms) compared to OGB-1.
source: For GCaMP6f (hSyn) the rise times exhibited slower kinetics (163 ± 14 ms, n = 30 traces, two animals, Figure 1J) presumably due to four calcium binding sites of the calmodulin, which need to be occupied to reach maximum fluorescence change, while similar values for durations and amplitudes of slow waves were observed as compared to OGB-1 (Figure 1K,L,M).
evidence: This statement reports quantitative experimental results for GCaMP6f and provides a mechanistic explanation.

claim: OGB-1 and GCaMP6f both reveal the same slow wave events with high correlation.
source: To test, whether indeed OGB-1 and GCaMP6f both reveal the same slow wave events, we conducted two-fiber experiments outside of the MR scanner, in two animals expressing GCaMP6f under control of the CaMKII promoter in S1FL, and being injected with OGB-1 2 mm posterior to that site on the same hemisphere. (Figure 1N). Indeed, we found the associated slow waves to be highly correlated (Figure 1N,O).
evidence: This statement reports experimental results from dual-fiber recordings.

claim: Population calcium transients are correlated with electrically recorded slow oscillations in the local field potentials.
source: In line with previous results (Busche et al., 2015; Stroh et al., 2013), the observed population calcium transients were correlated with electrically recorded slow oscillations in the local field potentials (LFPs; Figure 1P,Q).
evidence: This statement reports experimental results and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An average number of 298 ± 20 slow wave events per 30 min experiment were detected.
source: Applying this detection algorithm yielded an average number of 298 ± 20 slow wave events per 30 min experiment (n = 7 animals; Figure 2B).
evidence: This statement reports quantitative results from the detection algorithm.

claim: Averaged BOLD signal timecourses exhibited a sharp rise from baseline to maximum during 0.7 s ± 0.4 s after the onset of a slow calcium wave.
source: Timecourse of averaged HRs exhibited a sharp rise from baseline to maximum during 0.7 s ± 0.4 s after the onset of a slow calcium wave, reaching the maximum signal amplitude of 0.17%±0.03% (ΔSA) at 6.5 s ± 0.4 s (TTP) with a half maximum duration (HMD) of 6.8 s +- 0.5 s.
evidence: This statement reports quantitative characteristics of the hemodynamic response.

claim: Event-related fMRI analysis based on extracted HRFs revealed BOLD activation of nearly the entire cortex during slow wave activity in 6 of 8 experiments.
source: Using the detected individual slow wave events in the calcium signal in an event-related analysis based on extracted HRFs revealed BOLD activation of nearly the entire cortex during slow wave activity (Figure 3C,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) in 6 of 8 experiments (n = 7 rats).
evidence: This statement reports the primary finding of cortex-wide activation.

claim: Each cortical area showed at least partial BOLD activation predicted by slow calcium waves in every experiment.
source: While activation patterns were occasionally patchy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), each cortical area was showing at least partial BOLD activation predicted by slow calcium waves in every experiment, i.e. no cortical area was excluded from BOLD activity.
evidence: This statement reports the consistency of cortical activation across experiments.

claim: The F-values of somatosensory and visual cortex showed no significant differences in mean values.
source: The F-values of the two regions of the cortex showed no significant differences in mean values (Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement reports quantitative comparison results between cortical regions.

claim: No apparent differences in the shape of the hemodynamic responses could be observed between somatosensory and visual cortex.
source: In addition, we extracted the HR of the two regions from the beta-maps, no apparent differences in the shape of the HRs could be observed (p=0.23, Wilcoxon rank-sum test), indicative of a rather uniform activation profile throughout the cortex.
evidence: This statement reports statistical comparison results with a p-value.

claim: Swapping regressors between animals resulted in no BOLD activation.
source: To further test for the specificity and interrelation of a recorded calcium event array to the respective BOLD activation and to rule out a general effect of specifically spaced event-timing causing the reported effects, we applied two control procedures for this analysis: swapping regressors between the animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B) and temporally reverting the event arrays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D) resulted in no BOLD activation in any of the data sets, thus confirming the specificity of the observed activations.
evidence: This statement reports results from control experiments demonstrating specificity.

claim: Temporally reverting the event arrays resulted in no BOLD activation.
source: To further test for the specificity and interrelation of a recorded calcium event array to the respective BOLD activation and to rule out a general effect of specifically spaced event-timing causing the reported effects, we applied two control procedures for this analysis: swapping regressors between the animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B) and temporally reverting the event arrays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D) resulted in no BOLD activation in any of the data sets, thus confirming the specificity of the observed activations.
evidence: This statement reports results from control experiments demonstrating specificity.

claim: Slow wave events were recorded in the thalamus with similar characteristics compared to cortically recorded slow waves.
source: As expected, we were able to record typical slow wave events, albeit at a lower SNR (Figure 4B) in two animals, with similar characteristics compared to the cortically recorded slow waves, in line with a previous study (Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement reports experimental results from thalamic recordings and is supported by a citation.

claim: Using thalamic calcium waves as events revealed BOLD activation in the cortex only.
source: Using those thalamic calcium waves as events, we found BOLD activation in the cortex only (Figure 4E,F; 2 experiments in two animals), similar to the cortical recordings.
evidence: This statement reports experimental results from thalamic recordings.

claim: No BOLD signal in thalamus was detected, likely due to lower detection sensitivity of the MR surface coil in subcortical regions.
source: The fact that no BOLD signal in thalamus was detected is most likely due to using a MR surface coil which results in lower detection sensitivity in subcortical regions.
evidence: This statement provides an interpretation of the negative result based on technical limitations.

claim: ICA components mirrored the results obtained by using the slow calcium waves as regressor during ongoing slow wave activity.
source: With this analysis, during ongoing slow wave activity, we found ICA components mirroring the results obtained by using the slow calcium waves as regressor in the same animals (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement reports results from ICA analysis confirming the GLM results.

claim: The timecourse of the ICA component revealing cortex-wide activation is highly correlated with the GLM regressor obtained from slow wave onsets (R = 0.4 ± 0.05).
source: Notably, the timecourse of the ICA component revealing cortex-wide activation is highly correlated with the GLM regressor obtained from taking into account slow wave onsets detected in the calcium recordings (R = 0.4 ± 0.05, n = 9 animals; Figure 5B), further confirming the neurophysiological basis of this component.
evidence: This statement reports quantitative correlation results between ICA and GLM approaches.

claim: Cross-correlation of the ICA component timecourse with the temporally mirrored GLM-regressor leads to complete absence of correlation.
source: To test for specificity of those results we also calculated the same cross-correlation of the ICA component timecourse with the GLM-regressor, but with the GLM-regressor obtained from the temporally mirrored slow wave vector (see Figure 3—figure supplement 3C) of the same animal, which leads to a complete absence of correlation between the ICA component timecourse and the event-related GLM-regressor (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement reports results from a control analysis demonstrating specificity.

claim: Pan-cortical activation components were identified in both group- and single-subject based ICA results.
source: Notably, we could again identify pan-cortical activation patterns in both the group- and the single-subject based results (ICs #3, #6 in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement reports results from ICA analysis at different levels.

claim: The pan-cortical component exhibits higher power in the <0.1 Hz range.
source: A comparison of the power spectra related to the timecourses of the pan-cortical and two other components shows that the pan-cortical component exhibits higher power in the <0.1 Hz range (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This statement reports spectral analysis results characterizing the pan-cortical component.

claim: Regressing out the timecourse derived by the slow wave vector leads to complete absence of pan-cortical components in the ICA.
source: Regressing out the timecourse derived by the slow wave vector obtained from the calcium transients (see Materials and Methods), leads to complete absence of pan-cortical components in the ICA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This statement reports results from a control analysis demonstrating the specific contribution of slow waves.

claim: Electric forepaw stimulation reliably evoked slow waves locked to stimulus onset with a mean latency of 143 ms ± 7 ms.
source: For slow wave activity, we observed electric forepaw stimulation to reliably evoke slow waves locked to stimulus onset (A) with a mean latency of 143 ms ± 7 ms (30 events, three animals, (E), in reasonable agreement with studies in mice using visual or auditory stimulation (Grienberger et al., 2012; Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement reports experimental results from sensory stimulation experiments and is supported by citations.

claim: Stimulus-evoked calcium waves were not distinguishable from spontaneous waves.
source: Regarding signal characteristics, stimulus-evoked calcium waves were not distinguishable from spontaneous waves (H), again in agreement with previous studies (Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement reports experimental results comparing evoked and spontaneous waves and is supported by a citation.

claim: Slow waves followed all-or-none characteristics with a probability of induction of 72%±8%.
source: Waves followed all-or-none characteristics (A), with a probability of induction of 72%±8% (five animals, 12 traces).
evidence: This statement reports quantitative experimental results on slow wave induction.

claim: During persistent activity, neuronal calcium responses upon sensory stimuli had a significantly shorter latency of 20 ms ± 4 ms compared to slow wave state.
source: In the persistent activity condition, we detected neuronal calcium responses upon sensory stimuli with a significantly shorter latency of 20 ms ± 4 ms and a significantly shorter duration of 55 ms ± 3 ms, in agreement with previous studies (Schmid et al., 2016) versus 959 ms ± 36 ms in slow wave state (30 events, three animals, (E, F).
evidence: This statement reports quantitative experimental results comparing two conditions and is supported by a citation.

claim: Responses during persistent activity exhibited significantly shorter rise times compared to slow waves.
source: Responses during persistent activity exhibited significantly shorter rise times compared to slow waves (G), suggesting a different mechanism of activity initiation.
evidence: This statement reports experimental results and provides an interpretation.

claim: During persistent activity, no component indicative of a synchronous cortical activation was found.
source: During persistent activity, we did not find any component indicative of a synchronous cortical activation (n = 6), but we found resting state networks as previously described (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A,B) (Hsu et al., 2016; Jonckers et al., 2011; Kalthoff et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement reports negative results for persistent activity and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Using the somatosensory cortex as seed-ROI during ongoing slow wave activity revealed a correlating cortex-wide BOLD activation.
source: Using the somatosensory cortex as seed-ROI, during ongoing slow wave activity, we found a correlating cortex-wide BOLD activation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This statement reports results from seed-based analysis.

claim: The average signal in the somatosensory seed-ROI was strongly correlated with the normalized signal of the pan-cortical component revealed by ICA.
source: Furthermore, the average signal in the somatosensory seed-ROI was strongly correlated with the normalized signal of the pan-cortical component previously revealed by the ICA (Figure 6B; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This statement reports correlation results between seed-based and ICA approaches.

claim: During persistent activity, pan-cortical activity was absent in seed-based analysis.
source: During persistent activity this pan-cortical activity was absent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Figure 6—source data 1), but bilateral somatosensory activity, potentially reflecting inter-hemispheric connectivity between the somatosensory cortices (Hodkinson et al., 2016) could be detected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement reports negative results for persistent activity and is supported by a citation.

claim: During slow wave activity, voxel in the hippocampus correlate well with cortical voxel, spanning the entire cortical surface.
source: Indeed we occasionally observed hippocampal BOLD activation during slow waves and therefore conducted a seed-based analysis for an atlas-based hippocampal ROI, showing that voxel in the hippocampus correlate well with cortical voxel, again spanning the entire cortical surface during ongoing slow wave activity.
evidence: This statement reports results from hippocampal seed-based analysis.

claim: Correlation analysis revealed highest r-values for the entire cortex independent of the location of the somatosensory ROI.
source: When HRs upon slow calcium wave onsets in a ROI in somatosensory cortex are correlated with every remaining voxel in the brain, again a cortex-wide network becomes apparent. Independent of the location of the somatosensory ROI (right or left hemisphere) this correlation analysis revealed highest r-values for the entire cortex.
evidence: This statement reports results from calcium recordings-informed correlation analysis.

claim: Slow wave related BOLD activity recruits almost all cortical areas with nearly synchronous time-to-peak values for hemodynamic responses.
source: Additionally, correlation values reveal that slow wave related BOLD activity recruits almost all cortical areas with nearly synchronous time-to-peak values for HRs (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement reports results on the temporal characteristics of cortical recruitment.

claim: Locally recorded calcium events related to slow wave activity show a global cortical fMRI BOLD correlate.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate that locally recorded calcium events related to slow wave activity show a global cortical fMRI BOLD correlate.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion summarizing the main finding of the study.

claim: The novelty of the approach consists in establishing a direct relation of neurophysiologically defined slow wave events to the macroscopic fMRI signal.
source: The novelty of our approach consists in establishing a direct relation of neurophysiologically defined slow wave events to the macroscopic fMRI signal by detecting the precise time points of individual slow waves and probing their underlying hemodynamic responses by using event-related fMRI analysis.
evidence: This statement describes the novel contribution of the study.

claim: Under anesthesia, slow waves appear more rhythmic and more synchronous across the cortex compared to natural sleep.
source: Although the main features appear similar to those of the SWS oscillation (Destexhe et al., 2007; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017), under anesthesia, slow waves appear more rhythmic and more synchronous across the cortex and also show longer silence periods (Busche et al., 2015; Chauvette et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement compares anesthesia and sleep slow waves and is supported by citations.

claim: Sleep slow waves and anesthesia slow waves may recruit the same cortical and subcortical structures.
source: Nevertheless sleep slow waves and anesthesia slow waves may recruit the same cortical and subcortical structures (Murphy et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and uses the qualifier 'may', indicating it is a hypothesis.

claim: Slow waves are cortically generated.
source: Although cortically generated (Steriade et al., 1993c; Timofeev et al., 2000) slow waves also engage the thalamus (Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014; Steriade et al., 1993a; Stroh et al., 2013) and hippocampus (Busche et al., 2015; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Sirota et al., 2003), suggesting that slow wave associated excitation plays a synchronizing role in functional coupling of remote brain regions (Hahn et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing the origin of slow waves.

claim: Slow wave associated excitation plays a synchronizing role in functional coupling of remote brain regions.
source: Although cortically generated (Steriade et al., 1993c; Timofeev et al., 2000) slow waves also engage the thalamus (Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014; Steriade et al., 1993a; Stroh et al., 2013) and hippocampus (Busche et al., 2015; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Sirota et al., 2003), suggesting that slow wave associated excitation plays a synchronizing role in functional coupling of remote brain regions (Hahn et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and uses the qualifier 'suggesting', indicating it is an interpretation.

claim: Correlation of hippocampal activity to slow-wave related cortical BOLD might provide a mechanism of coordination for reactivation and redistribution of hippocampus-dependent memories to neocortical sites.
source: This correlation of hippocampal activity to slow-wave related cortical BOLD (Chan et al., 2017) might provide a mechanism of coordination for reactivation and redistribution of hippocampus-dependent memories to neocortical sites (Buzsáki, 1996; Mitra et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and uses the qualifier 'might', indicating it is a hypothesis.

claim: Anesthesia-related slow waves are unlikely to be involved in memory consolidation.
source: Although this is unlikely the case for anesthesia related slow waves (Murphy et al., 2011), they might recruit the same structures and thereby provide a spatiotemporal mechanism for such plasticity-relevant cortico-hippocampal functions (Logothetis et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and uses the qualifier 'unlikely', indicating it is an interpretation.

claim: Intracortically, slow waves can propagate as a travelling wave, likely by relays of local populations of cells.
source: Intracortically, slow waves can propagate as a travelling wave (Busche et al., 2015; Matsui et al., 2016; Stroh et al., 2013), likely by relays of local populations of cells (Destexhe et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and uses the qualifier 'likely', indicating it is a supported hypothesis.

claim: Depending on excitability state of the network, a slow wave event could either remain local or could spread.
source: Depending on excitability state of the network, a slow wave event could either remain local (Nir et al., 2011; Vyazovskiy et al., 2011) or could spread 'smoothly like an oil-spot' (Massimini et al., 2004; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing different propagation patterns.

claim: The recruitment of sub-cortical regions is discussed to rather involve long-range excitatory projections.
source: The recruitment of sub-cortical regions is discussed to rather involve long-range excitatory projections (Leong et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and uses the qualifier 'discussed to', indicating it is a hypothesis from the literature.

claim: This study bridges mesoscopic representation of slow waves in a defined population to the whole-brain hemodynamic BOLD signal.
source: Here, we bridge these mentioned levels of observation by relating the mesoscopic representation of slow waves in a defined cortical or thalamic population - in a spatio-temporally precise manner - to the whole-brain hemodynamic BOLD signal.
evidence: This statement describes the contribution of the study in bridging scales of observation.

claim: During persistent activity, seed-based analysis and ICA revealed typical default mode and resting state networks.
source: Here, seed-based analysis and ICA revealed typical default mode and resting state networks as described previously (Hsu et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement reports results for persistent activity and is supported by citations.

claim: The ICA component showing pan-cortical activation is highly correlated to the GLM timecourse derived from optically detected calcium waves.
source: Furthermore, during slow wave activity, we could demonstrate that the ICA component showing pan-cortical activation is highly correlated to the GLM timecourse derived from optically detected calcium waves.
evidence: This statement reports correlation results between ICA and GLM approaches.

claim: The pan-cortical component is related to higher power in the ultra-low frequency range.
source: Exclusively this pan-cortical component is related to higher power in the ultra-low frequency range.
evidence: This statement reports spectral characteristics of the pan-cortical component.

claim: Low frequency components were related to slow wave activity in spontaneous EEG/fMRI signal fluctuations in earlier studies.
source: Such low frequency components were related to slow wave activity in spontaneous EEG/fMRI signal fluctuations in earlier studies and have been investigated in different species (Leopold et al., 2003; Schölvinck et al., 2010; Steriade and Amzica, 1998; Wang et al., 2012; Wen and Liu, 2016)) including humans (Achermann and Borbély, 1997; Boly et al., 2012; Dang-Vu et al., 2008; Hiltunen et al., 2014; Marshall et al., 2006; Massimini et al., 2004; Wen and Liu, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work across species.

claim: If the timecourse derived from the slow wave vector is regressed out of the data, the ICA is devoid of any components showing pan-cortical activation.
source: Notably, if the timecourse derived from the slow wave vector is regressed out of the data, the ICA is devoid of any components showing pan-cortical activation.
evidence: This statement reports results from a control analysis demonstrating the specific contribution of slow waves.

claim: During ongoing slow wave activity, components resembling resting state networks can be identified.
source: Nonetheless, also during ongoing slow wave activity, we can identify components which likely resemble resting state networks, which seems reasonable, given that these networks are discussed to mirror basic functional connectivity.
evidence: This statement reports ICA results and provides an interpretation.

claim: Ongoing changes in network activity can contribute to the variability of experimental results and may appear as noise if disregarded in statistical modeling.
source: Ongoing changes in network activity can contribute to the variability of experimental results and may appear as noise if they are disregarded in the statistical modeling of neural signals (McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and discusses the importance of considering network states.

claim: A direct readout of neurophysiological measures may be beneficial to monitor and control for homogenous network activity states during BOLD measurements.
source: A direct readout of neurophysiological measures may also be beneficial to monitor and control for homogenous network activity states during BOLD measurements, as depth of anesthesia may vary depending on many physiological factors, as e.g. cortical temperature (Reig et al., 2010; Schwalm and Easton, 2016; Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and uses the qualifier 'may', indicating it is a recommendation.

claim: Including ongoing signals revealed by local neurophysiological readouts as a covariate could explain a considerable amount of variance in neuronal responses.
source: Including ongoing signals revealed by local neurophysiological readouts as an independent variable, i.e. covariate, regressor, or entirely new factor depending on the type of analysis, could explain a considerable amount of variance in neuronal responses, leading to more reliable readouts, especially in global measures as fMRI.
evidence: This statement uses the qualifier 'could', indicating it is a hypothesis about potential benefits.

claim: If there is a global participation of cortical areas in slow wave rhythmicity, the activity of the cellular population as a whole should produce a macroscopic signal detectable by functional neuroimaging.
source: We investigated the functional recruitment of brain areas by slow waves based on the reasoning that, if there is a global participation of cortical areas in slow wave rhythmicity, the activity of the cellular population as a whole should produce a macroscopic signal detectable by functional neuroimaging (Doeller et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement describes the reasoning behind the study and is supported by a citation.

claim: Results acquired with event-related analysis are in agreement with model-free and seed-based analysis approaches.
source: Results acquired with this method are in agreement with model-free and seed-based analysis approaches revealing a similar extension of network activity spanning almost the entire neocortex, also during ongoing slow wave activity.
evidence: This statement reports consistency across different analytical approaches.

claim: Spatio-temporal dynamics and behavioral correlates of slow waves in humans and animal models are highly preserved.
source: Our results provide a framework for further analysis of slow wave brain activity within fMRI experiments in anesthetized rodents or for EEG/fMRI studies at a translational level (Tagliazucchi et al., 2012), since spatio-temporal dynamics and behavioral correlates of slow waves in humans and animal models are highly preserved (Buzsáki et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and discusses translational relevance.

claim: There is growing evidence of impaired slow oscillations in models of Alzheimer disease.
source: For example, there is growing evidence of impaired slow oscillations in models of Alzheimer disease (Busche et al., 2015; Menkes-Caspi et al., 2015) and resting-state functional connectivity in Alzheimer patients (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on Alzheimer's disease.

claim: Calcium measures provide advantages in terms of spatial specificity and lack signal distortions by varying magnetic fields compared to electric population recordings.
source: Even though calcium measures provide advantages in terms of spatial specificity (Kajikawa and Schroeder, 2011) and lack signal distortions by the varying magnetic fields of the scanner in comparison to electric population recordings, our event-related approach could also be applied for combined EEG-fMRI measures feasible in human experiments.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and discusses methodological advantages.

claim: Experiments were conducted under isoflurane anesthesia (1.1–1.8%) inducing and maintaining slow wave activity.
source: Experiments were conducted under isoflurane anesthesia (1.1–1.8%) inducing and maintaining slow wave activity with recurrent slow wave events at similar frequencies (Chen et al., 2013b; Grienberger et al., 2012; Lissek et al., 2016; Luczak et al., 2007; Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement describes the experimental conditions and is supported by citations.

claim: The threshold for slow wave detection was set to 70% based on an inflection point in the number of active voxels.
source: To determine this threshold, amplitudes of all datapoints were sorted into a histogram. Onsets and durations for each threshold (in percent of maximum) were derived and the resulting numbers of active voxel of SPM-evaluations using these onsets and durations showed an inflection point at 70%, therefore the threshold was set to 70% for further evaluations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement describes the methodological decision for threshold selection based on data analysis.
